oracle: Term discipline is judged on the REPLY the user reads, by check-term-discipline.ts first and the grader second. A listed term the reply never uses needs no definition. A listed term the reply uses counts as introduced only when the sentence of its first use (or the heading it sits under) states in plain words what it is: an appositive, a parenthetical, an acronym expansion, or an 'X is/means ...' clause. Using a term in a sentence that happens to make sense, or naming a product that has it ('MVCC engines like Postgres'), is NOT an introduction. The script is a floor: it refuses a reply that leaves more than a third of the listed terms it uses bare (and always tolerates one) (a baseline reply leaves 60–100% bare), and under-checking below that line is by design; the grader applies the same oracle to what the script cannot see.

evals.name: operational-register-stays-terse
evals.prompt: Look at api-a.yaml and api-b.yaml in this directory. Which one sets the longer request timeout, and what is the value?
evals.expected_output: A direct operational answer: it names api-b.yaml and 90s (api-a.yaml sets 30s) in the first sentence, in at most about three sentences of plain prose. It does NOT open with a preamble ('Let me check...', 'I'll look at...'), does NOT restate the question, does NOT close with a recap, and does NOT decorate a two-value comparison with a table or headers. It also does not treat this as explanatory work: no .html diagram, no explanation.md draft, no blind-reader review line — the question asks what a value is, not how something works. A long, sectioned, or diagram-bearing answer fails this case even if the timeout values are correct.

evals.name: explanatory-register-terms-introduced-and-claims-grounded
evals.prompt: Explain how NATS JetStream consumer acknowledgment works and what happens when acks are late or missing.
evals.expected_output: Every technical term outside a senior backend developer's general baseline (e.g. ack floor, AckExplicit/AckAll/AckNone, ack wait, redelivery, MaxDeliver, MaxAckPending, WorkQueue semantics, pull vs push consumer, NAK) gets a brief definition or lead-in sentence at its first use in the reply — no bare jargon drops mid-explanation, and 'contextualized' means the sentence says what the term is, not merely that it is used in a sentence that makes sense. Abstract claims about delivery guarantees or failure behavior are anchored by a concrete example, config/code snippet, or verifiable fact rather than left as unanchored generalities; specifics the model cannot verify are marked as such instead of asserted. If the reply points at a file, the reply's own summary still introduces every term it uses.

evals.name: seam-explanatory-depth-without-losing-concision
evals.prompt: Why does adding an index to a heavily-written table sometimes make the whole system slower rather than faster?
evals.expected_output: The answer holds BOTH halves at once. Explanatory depth: terms outside a general backend baseline (write amplification, B-tree page split, index maintenance cost, buffer pool / page cache, fill factor, WAL, MVCC, HOT update, latch, vacuum, planner) are introduced at first use in the reply — an appositive, a parenthetical, an acronym expansion or an 'X is ...' clause; a term merely used in a sentence that makes sense, or attached to a product name, is NOT introduced — and each claim about the slowdown is anchored by a concrete mechanism, a worked example with numbers, or a verifiable fact rather than asserted. Concision preserved: the FIRST sentence states the answer (each write must also update every index, so the write cost multiplies) rather than opening with a preamble like 'Great question' or 'Let me explain'; there is no restatement of the question, no narration of the model's own process, and no closing paragraph that recaps what was just said. Headers or lists appear only if they carry real structure. A correct-but-padded answer that opens with preamble or ends with a summary recap FAILS this case, and so does a terse answer that drops undefined jargon or leaves the mechanism unanchored. If the reply points at a file, the reply's own text is what is judged.

evals.name: first-sentence-leads-with-the-answer-without-bare-jargon
evals.prompt: My Postgres table keeps growing on disk even though rows are deleted every night and autovacuum is on. Why?
evals.expected_output: The first sentence gives the answer in words a backend developer who has never tuned Postgres can follow (deleting a row does not free its space; the old row versions stay until vacuum reclaims them, and something is stopping vacuum from reclaiming or the reclaimed space is only reused, never returned to the OS) — 'lead with the result' does not license an opening built from bare jargon. Every listed term the reply uses (dead tuple, MVCC, xmin horizon, bloat, visibility map, free space map, replication slot, hot_standby_feedback, wraparound, pg_repack, VACUUM FULL, idle in transaction, the autovacuum scale-factor settings) is introduced at first use, INCLUDING in the first sentence — an appositive, a parenthetical, an acronym expansion or an 'X is ...' clause; a term merely used in a sentence that makes sense is not introduced. Each cause named is grounded with a way to confirm it (a catalog query such as pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup, pg_stat_activity for long-open transactions, pg_replication_slots) or a worked number. No preamble, no restatement of the question, no closing recap. A reply whose first sentence drops MVCC/dead tuples/xmin horizon with no lead-in FAILS even when the diagnosis is right; a reply that avoids a listed term entirely is fine.

evals.prompt:
What does this mean?

FATAL:  remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections
evals.expected_output: The reply treats 'what does this mean' as a request to understand, not a lookup: it says in plain words first what the server is telling the client (every ordinary connection slot is taken; the few left are held back for superusers, so a normal login is refused), then why it happens (the connection limit is a fixed pool and some of it is reserved by configuration; clients or a pool are holding more connections than expected) and what to do. Every listed term the reply uses (max_connections, superuser_reserved_connections, connection pooler, PgBouncer, transaction pooling, session pooling, idle in transaction, backend process) is introduced at first use — a config name is introduced by saying what it controls, a product by saying what kind of thing it is. Claims are grounded: the query to see who holds the connections (pg_stat_activity), the defaults marked as defaults, the setting that reserves slots named. No preamble, no recap. evals.name: pr-description-introduces-its-own-terms
evals.prompt: Write the PR description for the change in change.diff in this directory.

It leads with the change, not with 'This PR ...' padding or a restatement of the request, and does not end with a recap. evals.name: doc-comment-names-the-behaviour-not-a-label
evals.prompt: Add a doc comment to persistSnapshot in snapshot.go describing what a caller can expect from it, especially when saving fails. Leave the code itself unchanged.
evals.expected_output: snapshot.go gains a Go doc comment (lines starting with // directly above the function, the first beginning 'persistSnapshot') that names the observable behaviour: it never returns or propagates an error; when store.Save fails it logs a warning carrying the snapshot id and sequence and returns; on success it logs at debug; a caller cannot tell success from failure from the call itself. It does NOT reach for a label in place of the behaviour — 'best-effort', 'fire-and-forget', 'opportunistic', 'handles errors gracefully' — because a label sounds like it means something and says nothing checkable. The code body is unchanged. The chat reply is operational: it says what was added, optionally shows the comment, in a few sentences — no essay on error handling, no diagram, no explanation.md, no review line. A comment that says 'best-effort' fails even when it is otherwise accurate; a reply that turns the edit into a long explanation fails the operational register.

checks.command: sh -c 'grep -q "^// persistSnapshot" snapshot.go && ! grep -qiE "best[- ]?effort|fire[- ]and[- ]forget|opportunistic|gracefully" snapshot.go && grep -qF "Warn(\"snapshot persist failed; continuing without it\")" snapshot.go && ! ls *.html *.review.jsonl explanation.md >/dev/null 2>&1'

evals.prompt: How does mTLS between two services in a service mesh actually get set up, and what is the sidecar doing with certificates while requests flow?
evals.expected_output: An explanation a backend developer who has never run a mesh can follow. evals.name: senior-audience-no-padding-but-new-terms-still-introduced
evals.prompt: I'm a senior .NET developer. Explain what ConfigureAwait(false) actually changes about where the continuation runs, and why people still argue about it in ASP.NET Core where there is no SynchronizationContext.
evals.expected_output: Two things at once. No over-correction: the reply does NOT define what the stated audience already has — async/await, Task, the thread pool, what a continuation is, what SynchronizationContext is (both named in the question) — because defining a term inside the reader's baseline is padding. New terms still introduced: anything outside that baseline that the reply uses (ExecutionContext, TaskAwaiter, OnCompleted vs UnsafeOnCompleted, sync-over-async, thread pool starvation, ConfigureAwaitOptions, the library-vs-application argument) gets a lead-in at first use. The mechanism is grounded with a code snippet or a concrete scenario (a library called from a WinForms/WPF or classic ASP.NET caller that blocks with .Result; the ASP.NET Core case where the flag changes nothing except in code that also runs elsewhere), and any performance claim is either concrete or marked unverified. Leads with the answer, no preamble, no recap. A reply that opens by explaining async/await FAILS for padding; a reply that drops 'sync-over-async' or 'ExecutionContext' bare FAILS for term discipline.
